title: Strong suppression of the photonic density of states in three-dimensional disordered silicon networks
authors: Abraham Aguilar Uribe, Francisco Hernández Alejandre, Mattis Reisner, Geoffroy Aubry, Luis S. Froufe-Pérez, Marian Florescu, Frank Scheffold
abstract: Photonic bandgaps can open not only in crystalline dielectric materials but also in amorphous structures. Self-uniform amorphous gyroid networks have been proposed as promising disordered photonic architectures. Motivated by numerical studies, we combine direct laser-writing lithography with advanced materials processing to fabricate these structures from high-refractive-index silicon. Spectroscopic measurements at mid-infrared wavelengths reveal pronounced transmission minima. To investigate the formation of photonic band gaps in amorphous structures, we develop polarization-resolved transmission spectroscopy that separates ballistic and multiply scattered contributions, enabling direct identification of the underlying transport regimes. We observe a strong suppression of diffuse transmission, providing direct experimental evidence for a breakdown of conventional diffuse transport associated with a strongly reduced photonic density of states. Together with large-scale numerical simulations, our results establish the presence of a deep photonic pseudogap in an amorphous three-dimensional dielectric material and open new opportunities for observing disorder-induced localization phenomena, including Anderson localization of light.
summary: This paper reports the experimental observation of a deep photonic pseudogap in amorphous, disordered silicon networks using advanced lithography and polarization-resolved spectroscopy. By separating ballistic and diffuse light components, the authors provide direct evidence for the breakdown of classical diffuse transport, confirming the existence of disorder-induced light localization.
main_problem: The study investigates the formation and characterization of photonic band gaps (or pseudogaps) in amorphous, disordered dielectric structures, moving beyond the traditional reliance on long-range periodicity.
main_result: The authors experimentally establish the presence of a deep photonic pseudogap in an amorphous 3D dielectric by observing a strong suppression of diffuse transmission, indicating a breakdown of conventional diffuse transport.
method: The research combines advanced fabrication (DLW lithography) with polarization-resolved transmission spectroscopy to separate ballistic and multiply scattered light contributions for diagnosis.
model_or_system: The physical system is a three-dimensional disordered silicon network, specifically amorphous gyroid networks, fabricated with a controlled volume filling fraction. The analysis compares experimental measurements with large-scale numerical simulations (FDTD) solving Maxwell's equations.
key_observables: Transmission spectra ($T_{int}(L)$), diffuse transmission ($T_d(L)$), ballistic transmission ($T_b(L)$), and the scattering mean free path ($\ell_s(\lambda)$).
important_parameters: Gap center wavelength ($\lambda_{	ext{gap}} \approx 4.7 \mu	ext{m}$), volume filling fraction ($\phi \approx 20-25\%$), and the Ioffe–Regel parameter.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating ballistic and diffuse light contributions using polarization-resolved spectroscopy, and the simulation/analysis assumes the cross-polarized signal is negligible for estimating $T_b(L)$.
figures_summary: Figures show the fabricated structure, optical characterization setups, and spectral plots demonstrating the transmission minimum (pseudogap) and the dependence of transmission components on sample thickness.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the feasibility of photonic bandgaps in amorphous materials to detailing the advanced spectroscopic techniques required to diagnose the gap by analyzing transport breakdown, culminating in quantitative agreement between experiment and simulation.
why_interesting: The work provides a direct experimental realization and diagnostic method for observing light localization phenomena (analogous to Anderson localization) in disordered media, which is a key topic in condensed matter physics and quantum optics.
